title: Psalm 97: The LORD Reigns in Cloud and Fire
summary: The psalm announces that the LORD reigns and describes his appearing in the images of storm and volcano: cloud and darkness, fire, lightning, and mountains melting like wax. Idol worshipers are put to shame, while Zion rejoices at his judgments. The psalm closes by calling those who love the LORD to hate evil, trust his protection, and rejoice in him.
story: This is the third of the kingship psalms that follow Psalm 95 (Psalms 96 to 99), each opening or turning on the claim that the LORD reigns. Psalm 96 invited the nations to worship the coming Judge. Psalm 97 shows what his coming looks like, drawing on the memory of Sinai, where God first appeared to Israel in fire and cloud, and then turns to what it means for the faithful. Book IV of the Psalter is responding to the loss of the Davidic kingdom by pointing to the King who was ruling before David and will rule after him; this psalm pictures that King arriving in power.
historical:
Psalm 97 has no heading in Hebrew, and nothing in it names a king or an event. Like the other kingship psalms, it was probably sung in the temple in Jerusalem, and many scholars connect these psalms with the autumn Festival of Tabernacles (Booths), when Israel celebrated the harvest and remembered the wilderness years. The Norwegian scholar Sigmund Mowinckel argued in the 1920s that Israel held a yearly festival celebrating the LORD's enthronement, modeled in part on Babylonian new-year rites; others accept a festival setting but doubt the enthronement ceremony he reconstructed, and still others read these psalms as looking forward to God's final reign rather than reenacting it.

The psalm draws on older texts almost line by line. Its imagery of cloud, darkness, fire, and melting mountains echoes the Sinai story (Exodus 19) and poems such as Judges 5, Psalm 18, and Micah 1:4. Several phrases also match the prophecies of Isaiah 40 to 55. For that reason many scholars date it after the exile, composed by a poet steeped in Israel's earlier Scriptures; others think a shared stock of temple language explains the overlap.
cultural:
The storm was the standard way ancient Near Eastern peoples pictured a god on the march. Baal, the Canaanite storm god, was described riding the clouds and thundering, and hymns to other gods also used lightning and shaking mountains. Israel's poets used the same imagery deliberately, claiming for the LORD what their neighbors claimed for their gods, and then adding what the others lacked: “righteousness and justice are His throne’s foundation” (verse 2). The throne of a king in that world stood on a raised base; this King's throne rests on moral order, not raw power.

“The distant shores” (verse 1) were the islands and coastlands of the Mediterranean, the farthest places an Israelite could imagine. “The towns of Judah” (verse 8) are literally the daughters of Judah, the villages around Jerusalem. The line “Worship Him, all you gods” (verse 7) addresses the powers the nations worshiped, whatever they were; the Greek translation rendered it as a call to God's angels.
literary: The psalm moves in three stages. Verses 1 to 6 are a theophany, a description of God appearing, told in the imagery of storm and fire, framed by the earth rejoicing (verse 1) and all peoples seeing his glory (verse 6). Verses 7 to 9 show the two responses to that appearing: shame for those who worship images, joy for Zion. Verses 10 to 12 turn to exhortation, moving from the cosmic scale to the ordinary life of the faithful. Light runs through the psalm as a thread: lightning lights the world in verse 4, and in verse 11 light is sown, like seed, for the righteous. The ending returns to the rejoicing of the opening, now focused on God's people.

outline.t: The LORD appears in cloud, fire, and lightning
Idolaters ashamed, Zion glad, the LORD Most High
Those who love the LORD: hate evil and rejoice

doctrines.note: Cloud and darkness surround God because he cannot be seen or handled; fire goes before him because he is dangerous to evil. The psalm holds together his hiddenness and his blazing presence.
God's reign rests on righteousness and justice. His kingship is not arbitrary force but moral rule, which is why the righteous welcome it and idolaters are shamed by it.
Those who boast in idols are put to shame when the true God appears. Worship aimed at anything less than the Most High ends in embarrassment.

words.note: Araphel, thick cloud or deep darkness. It is the word used for the dark cloud where God was at Sinai (Exodus 20:21; Deuteronomy 4:11). Paired here with the ordinary word for cloud, it signals that the King who reigns is the God of Sinai, present but veiled.

Makon, foundation or fixed place. Used of the base of a throne or of God's dwelling place. The claim that righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne (also in Psalm 89:14) says what his rule stands on.

Elyon, Most High. An old title for God (Genesis 14:18-22) that places him above every other power. Verse 9 uses it to make the psalm's central claim: the LORD is Most High over all the earth and far above all gods.

Chasid, faithful or godly one, translated “saints” in verse 10. It is related to chesed, God's covenant love, and describes people who answer that love with loyalty. The saints in the Psalms are not a spiritual elite but ordinary faithful Israelites.

christ: Hebrews 1:6 says that when God brings his firstborn into the world, he says, in effect, let all God's angels worship him. Scholars debate whether the writer is quoting the Greek form of this psalm's verse 7 or the Greek text of Deuteronomy 32:43, which has a similar line; either way, Hebrews applies to the Son words that in the Old Testament call heavenly beings to worship the LORD. That is a striking claim about who Jesus is. The New Testament also uses the imagery of cloud and fire for Christ's return (for example 2 Thessalonians 1:7-8), so the church has read this psalm's picture of the LORD's appearing as a picture of the day when the King is revealed.

hard.q: Why does a psalm about God's goodness tell people to hate?
hard.a: Verse 10 commands those who love the LORD to hate evil, and some readers find the language of hatred uncomfortable anywhere in worship. But the object is evil, not people, and the logic is simple: to love someone who is good is to reject what harms and opposes that goodness. Indifference to evil would be the real failure of love. The psalm also refuses to make the faithful into avengers; it is God who preserves, delivers, and judges. Harder questions arise in psalms that speak of hating enemies (Psalm 139:21-22, for example), and readers differ on how to take those; this verse keeps its focus on evil itself.

questions: The psalm says God is surrounded by cloud and darkness and also that his lightning lights the world. How do God's hiddenness and his clarity both show up in your experience?
What does it look like to love God and hate evil at the same time without becoming self-righteous?
Verse 11 pictures light as something sown for the righteous. What might it mean that joy is planted and grows rather than arriving all at once?
